chapters.title: Chapter 1: A different way to respond
chapters.intro: You've recognized that when certain remarks are directed at you, you feel tension in your body. This causes you to react by either freezing, wanting to run away or counter-attacking the person who expressed these remarks. You take a test to see if you can determine what you could have done differently to handle the exchange more confidently and serenely.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: My first Dojo
chapters.intro: You've drummed up the courage to go to the VA dojo, where practitioners of all ages and styles welcome you warmly. After various warm-up activities including a salutation, a centering and a 'Verbal Stretching' you feel ready to go on the 'Verbal Mat' and test your reflexes. The attack for today is 'You're so selfish'.

Really? Wow, I'm sorry, I didn't mean to be.
What do you mean?

lessons.title: Spotting the Four Reactive Responses
lessons.summary: Learn to recognize Justify, Counter-attack, Flight and Submissive/Victim/Negating reactions — the reflexes that escalate an exchange like "You always think you're right about everything!".

media.label: Article: Why we justify, counter-attack or flee (placeholder)

body: When someone says "You always think you're right about everything!", most of us don't reply — we react. In Verbal Aikido these reflexes are called the reactive responses: Justify (defending your position), Counter-attack (returning the aggression), and Flight (escaping the exchange).

There are also quieter forms of the same reflex: Submissive (giving in to stop the discomfort), Victim play (making yourself the injured party), and Negating emotion (denying or minimizing what the other person feels).

None of these are 'bad' — they are protection mechanisms. But each one either escalates the attacker's energy or abandons your own position. The Aikido response is different: it accepts the incoming energy and redirects it toward a real conversation.

In Chapter 1 you saw this in action: every non-Aikido reply kept the loop going, while the Aikido reply — acknowledging the grain of truth and inviting the other person to say more — created an energy shift.

quiz.question: Your partner says "You always think you're right!" and you reply "No I don't, I agreed with you a minute ago!" Which reactive response is this?
quiz.explanation: Defending your position with evidence is Justify — it keeps the dispute about who is right.

quiz.question: Replying "Well, if you didn't make so many mistakes, I wouldn't have to correct you!" is an example of…
quiz.explanation: Returning the aggression is Counter-attack — it raises the anger meter.

quiz.question: What makes the reply "I do often think I'm right, yes. Tell me more about what's going on with you though." an Aikido response?
choices: It accepts part of the attack and redirects toward dialogue
It apologizes so the attack stops
quiz.explanation: Aikido accepts the incoming energy (the grain of truth) and redirects it into a conversation instead of resisting or escalating.

lessons.title: The Verbal Mat: De-escalating "You're so selfish"
lessons.summary: Practice reading the exchange on the Verbal Mat: how centered listening, open questions and reflecting back turn "You're so selfish!" into a conversation.

media.label: Video: A round on the Verbal Mat (placeholder)
Article: Open questions as a de-escalation move (placeholder)

body: In the dojo, the 'Verbal Mat' is where you spar with words. The attack "You're so selfish!" is a classic opener: it is a judgment about your character, not a request.

Reactive replies make it worse. Counter-attacking ("You're the selfish one!") spikes the anger to breaking point. Submitting ("I'm sorry, I didn't mean to be") abandons your ground and invites a harder follow-up.

The Aikido move is an open question — "What do you mean?", "When did you first start to feel that way?", "What would you prefer to happen?". Each one moves the exchange from accusation toward information.
Notice the rhythm in Chapter 2: even a partial success ("Hmm. OK… let's pick this up later.") counts as an energy shift. De-escalation is a practice, not a perfect score.

quiz.question: Why is "What do you mean?" an effective first reply to "You're so selfish!"?
choices: It challenges the attacker to prove their claim
It is an open question that invites the attacker to explain instead of escalate
It agrees that you are selfish
quiz.explanation: Open questions are the core Aikido move: they accept the energy of the attack and redirect it into useful information.

quiz.question: "Really? Wow, I'm sorry, I didn't mean to be." is which response type?
quiz.explanation: Apologizing to stop the discomfort is Submissive — it abandons your position and usually invites another attack.

quiz.question: On the Verbal Mat, a reply that ends with "Hmm. OK… let's pick this up later." is scored as…
choices: A partial success — an energy shift worth repeating
quiz.explanation: Partial success still shifts the energy of the exchange; the PDF says it's 'worth doing again (repeat)'.

stretching.intro: Stretching exercises train the listening muscle. Posture 1 (expression) is guided by the bot; Posture 2 (listening) is for practice with a partner.

posture1.title: Posture 1 — Expression (guided by bot)
questions: What is the attack or criticism you heard most recently?
What did you feel in your body when you heard it?
What did you want to say back in the moment?
What might the other person actually need underneath the attack?
What would an Aikido-style reply sound like for you?

posture2.title: Posture 2 — Listening (with a partner)
questions: Repeat back what you heard without correcting it.
Name the emotion you hear underneath the words.
Ask one open question about what they need.
Summarize their position so they say "yes, that's it."
posture2.note: Practice live with a partner. Write notes below about what you observed.

sparring.intro: The sparring bot throws random attacks at you. Self-assess each reply type to build reflexes. Requires completing a Discovery lesson first (knowledge gate).
attacks: You never listen to anyone but yourself!
Why do you always have to be so dramatic?
Everyone thinks you messed this up, you know.
You call that an apology? Pathetic.
You always ruin everything you touch.
Stop pretending you care about this project.
You think you are better than everyone else.
sparring.tip: An Aikido response acknowledges the attack, then redirects toward what the attacker needs — e.g. "Sounds like this really matters to you. What would you want to see happen?"
